region: Pelvic girdle, thigh, leg and foot
note: Serial correspondences to forelimb muscles are recorded in `homology.serial`. Following Diogo & Molnar (2014), a listed correspondence is a claim of TOPOLOGICAL equivalence only. It is not a claim of serial homology in the strict (ancestral-duplication) sense, and in several documented cases the two muscles derive from different anlagen.

muscles.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the pelvic limb bud.
synonyms: puboischiofemoralis internus A–D (Prikryl et al. 2009 letter codes, anurans)

consensus.origin: Internal (medial) surface of the pubis and ilium, and the ventral surfaces of the posterior trunk vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, on or near the trochanter.
consensus.action: Protracts (flexes) and medially rotates the femur; the principal hip protractor of sprawling tetrapods.
consensus.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2–L4) and direct branches of the lumbar plexus.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
occurrences.origin: Internal (dorsal) face of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Extensively on the femur — the anterior face, extending dorsally and ventrally — anterior to the puboischiofemoralis externus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Passes anterior to the ilium to reach the hip. The pubo-ischiac plate is the fused ventral pelvic plate; it is scored here as pubis plus ischium, following the paper's own gloss of the ischium as the plate's posterior portion.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus A–D
occurrences.note: Prikryl et al. (2009) letter codes are used deliberately in place of the mammalian-sounding names ('iliacus', 'sartorius', 'pectineus') that earlier authors applied to these muscles, because those names imply homologies that do not hold. The anuran iliacus externus and internus belong to this field. Note the unresolved 'pectineus' — Noble (1922) placed it here, others in the externus.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis internus + iliotrochantericus cranialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian puboischiofemoralis internus 1-2. Hip flexors and medial rotators; Allen et al. find hip medial-rotator moment arms roughly doubling along the bird line.

occurrences.name: Iliacus + psoas major (+ sartorius)
occurrences.origin: Iliac fossa; bodies and transverse processes of T12–L5.
occurrences.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur.
occurrences.action: Flexes the hip; the principal hip flexor.
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar follow Walker & Homberger (1997) in deriving the mammalian sartorius from the ANTERIOR HEAD of puboischiofemoralis internus — not from the reptilian 'ambiens', as is commonly stated.

parts.name: Sartorius
parts.note: Diogo & Molnar follow Walker & Homberger (1997) in deriving it from the anterior head of this muscle, against the common claim that it comes from the reptilian 'ambiens'.

homology.notes: A stable row across Tetrapoda. Its subdivision in mammals into iliacus, psoas major and sartorius is a derived elaboration.

serial.caution: Topological correspondence only — the pelvic and pectoral internal girdle muscles were not acquired at the same time.

homology.teaching: The sartorius derivation is a good correction to a widespread textbook claim.

muscles.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) mass.

consensus.origin: External (lateral/ventral) surfaces of the pubis and ischium.
consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, ventrally.
consensus.action: Adducts and laterally rotates the femur.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Deeply blended with the 'pubofemoralis' (= adductor femoris) in Necturus (Walker 1954).
occurrences.origin: Much of the ventral surface of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral surface of the femur, over nearly two-thirds of the bone's length.
occurrences.attachmentNote: An insertion covering two-thirds of the femoral shaft. Extensive fleshy attachments like this one are why femoral muscle scars in salamanders are poor guides to muscle boundaries.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Přikryl et al. (2009) note that the anuran 'pectineus' was identified as puboischiofemoralis EXTERNUS by Hoffmann (1873-78) and Iordansky & Morozov (1994), but as puboischiofemoralis INTERNUS by Noble (1922). The primary literature disagrees about which of the two it is, not merely about what to call it.

occurrences.name: M. obturatorius lateralis + medialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian puboischiofemoralis externus 1-3.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Reconstructed from the ventral pelvic plate and the trochanteric region; its relative size is one of the variables Bishop & Pierce use to infer posture.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus, quadratus femoris, gemelli
occurrences.origin: External surface of the obturator membrane and adjacent pubis and ischium.
occurrences.insertion: Trochanteric fossa of the femur.
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the thigh; stabilises the hip.
occurrences.divisionNote: The gemelli are claimed by this field and by the ischiotrochantericus; the dataset records both claims.

homology.notes: The obturator nerve is the constant marker for this field across Tetrapoda.

muscles.name: Iliofemoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, on or near the greater trochanter.
consensus.action: Abducts the femur; in erect-limbed taxa, the principal hip abductor and pelvic stabiliser during single-limb support.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the anterior iliac blade, sharing an intramuscular septum with the puboischiotibialis; the belly wraps the posterior femoral border to insert proximally. Femur abductor, active in swing.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin on the lateral ilium; the femorotibialis internus tendon arises distal and anterior to it, which is the landmark Klinkhamer et al. use to separate the two.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Hip abductor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.note: Its expansion, tracked through the enlargement of the iliac blade, is central to Bishop & Pierce's argument that erect hindlimb posture was acquired late in the therian stem lineage.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Expansion of the iliac blade along the synapsid stem tracks the enlargement of this field and the shift toward erect posture.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius + gluteus minimus
occurrences.origin: Gluteal surface of the ilium.
occurrences.insertion: Greater trochanter of the femur.
occurrences.action: Abduct and medially rotate the thigh; prevent pelvic drop during the stance phase.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Same muscle, same nerve, same attachments — but in a parasagittal limb it becomes the principal pelvic stabiliser during single-limb support.

homology.notes: Universal in Tetrapoda. The functional transformation — from a modest abductor in a sprawling limb to the principal pelvic stabiliser in a parasagittal one — happens without any change in identity, origin, insertion or nerve.
homology.teaching: The best single muscle for showing that posture change is a change in mechanics, not in anatomy. Same muscle, same nerve, radically different role.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Caudofemoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; derived from the caudal axial musculature, not from the limb bud proper.

consensus.origin: Ventrolateral surfaces of the caudal vertebrae and their transverse processes (longus); the posterolateral ilium (brevis).
consensus.insertion: Fourth trochanter of the femur.
consensus.action: The principal femoral retractor of non-mammalian tetrapods — the main propulsive muscle of the hindlimb in sprawling and archosaurian locomotion.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the caudal spinal nerves; inferior gluteal nerve territory in mammals.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.origin: Transverse processes of the fourth and fifth caudal vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the femur, by a strong tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The origin has a countable segmental address — caudals four and five — which is rare in this dataset and is what makes the caudofemoralis tractable in fossils. The insertion is given as the femoral crista ventralis; whether that ridge is the same structure as the amniote fourth trochanter is not settled here, so no landmark is asserted.

occurrences.note: Reduced with the loss of the tail; the urostyle replaces the caudal series.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.action: Primary femoral retractor; drives the propulsive stroke in lizard locomotion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Longus arises from the proximal third of the tail and caudal vertebrae 4-14, inserting by broad tendon on the femoral trochanter plus a second tendon onto the lateral menisci of the knee; brevis arises from the transverse processes of the four most anterior postsacral vertebrae. Femur retraction and long-axis rotation, active in stance.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Large and well developed; inserts on a prominent fourth trochanter.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Klinkhamer et al. distinguish caudofemoralis longus (caudal vertebrae) from brevis (ilium); both converge on the fourth trochanter.

occurrences.name: M. caudofemoralis pars caudalis + pars pelvica
occurrences.note: Greatly reduced with the shortening of the tail to the pygostyle and the shift to a knee-driven, femur-held-horizontal gait. Its reduction is a defining event in the theropod–bird locomotor transition. Allen et al. (2021) split the avian muscle into pars caudalis (= crocodylian caudofemoralis longus) and pars pelvica (= brevis). Its leverage declines across several nodes along the bird line.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.note: Progressive reduction along the synapsid stem, tracked through the reduction of the fourth trochanter.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Progressive reduction of the fourth trochanter along the synapsid stem tracks the loss of tail-driven femoral retraction.

occurrences.note: Largely lost; the fourth trochanter is absent. A caudofemoralis persists in some marsupials and in taxa with muscular tails. The piriformis has been proposed as a remnant.

homology.notes: Presence and size track the fourth trochanter directly, making this the most reliably reconstructed hindlimb muscle in fossils. Its independent reduction in birds and in mammals accompanies two separate shifts away from tail-driven femoral retraction.

serial.caution: No forelimb counterpart. The caudofemoralis is a clean falsification of any expectation of one-to-one fore/hindlimb correspondence.

homology.teaching: The single best fossil-muscle example: a bony landmark (the fourth trochanter) that reads directly as muscle presence, size and locomotor mode across 300 million years.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Extensor iliotibialis / iliotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.insertion: Tibia, via the knee extensor apparatus.
consensus.action: Extends the knee; protracts the femur.

occurrences.name: Extensor iliotibialis
occurrences.note: Single-headed in Taricha, against the two heads (pars anterior and posterior) usual in Cryptobranchus, Necturus, Salamandra, Pseudoeurycea, Ambystoma and Dicamptodon. The split tracks limb robustness rather than habitat or phylogeny: slender-limbed salamanders (Amphiuma, Typhlomolge, Bolitoglossa, Taricha) have one head, robust-limbed ones two, and aquatic and terrestrial species occur in both groups. Smith (1927) reported two heads in the congener Taricha granulosa, so the character may vary within the genus.
occurrences.origin: Lateral surface of the ilium above the acetabulum.
occurrences.insertion: Spine of the tibia, by a long strong tendon.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crosses both hip and knee. Recorded with a single head in Taricha; the tibial insertion is on the anterior proximal tibia, which the paper calls the spine and which may or may not be the cnemial crest of amniotes — left unasserted.

occurrences.name: Extensor iliotibialis A/B
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar use letter codes rather than the mammalian names ('gluteus maximus', 'tensor fasciae latae') applied by earlier authors, because those homologies do not hold. Přikryl et al. (2009) list the anuran muscle as 'glutaeus maximus (iliotibialis)'. It is NOT homologous with the mammalian gluteus maximus — one of the twelve false-friend names Diogo & Molnar (2014) identify.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iliotibialis 3 arises deep to iliotibialis 2 on the central lateral ilium by tendon and inserts fleshy onto the distal third of the dorso-lateral femur.

occurrences.name: M. iliotibialis cranialis + lateralis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian iliotibialis 1-3.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris + tensor fasciae latae
occurrences.origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine (rectus femoris); iliac crest (tensor fasciae latae).
occurrences.insertion: Patella and tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament; iliotibial tract.
occurrences.action: Extends the knee; flexes the hip.
occurrences.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2–L4); superior gluteal nerve (tensor fasciae latae).

homology.notes: The urodele/reptile correspondence is actively disputed. Kardong (2002) derives the reptilian femorotibialis, iliotibialis and 'ambiens' from three distinct salamander muscles; Gadow (1882), Walker (1954) and Diogo & Molnar derive all three from a single salamander extensor iliotibialis. The dissections in Diogo & Molnar (2014) support the latter.
homology.openQuestion: One salamander muscle or three? The answer changes how many separate acquisitions are needed in the reptile lineage.

serial.caution: Both are the principal extensor of the second limb joint, but the correspondence is functional and topological, not developmental.

homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Iliofibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass.

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the ilium, posterior to the iliofemoralis origin.
consensus.insertion: Proximal fibula, via a broad tendon.
consensus.action: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; stabilises the femur during the stance phase.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.origin: Posterior abdominal margin of the ilium.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal tibia via a broad tendon.
occurrences.note: Tomańska et al. (2025) report it stabilising the pelvic region and femur during movement in Varanus komodoensis, allowing hip abduction. Dick & Clemente (2016) include it among the major varanid locomotor muscles.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Its insertion marks the iliofibular tubercle on the fibular shaft, which Pereyra et al. (2024) use as the landmark for the fibularis longus origin.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Name retained across the crocodylian–avian transition. Allen et al. (2021) find knee-flexor leverage declining relative to knee extensors along the bird line, which is the leverage change underlying the shift from hip-driven to knee-driven propulsion.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Present in anurans under the same name; Přikryl et al. (2009) describe it attaching to the knee aponeurosis, partly covering the head of the fibula.

occurrences.name: Iliofibularis
occurrences.origin: External face of the ilium, just posterior to the extensor iliotibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior side of the proximal end of the fibula, by a tendon.
occurrences.action: Elevates the femur and flexes the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Runs parallel to the extensor iliotibialis but slightly deeper and posterior, crossing both hip and knee. The insertion is the site the iliofibular tubercle marks in taxa that have one; no landmark is asserted here because the paper does not name a tubercle.

homology.notes: One of the muscles whose name survives unchanged from crocodylians to birds in Allen et al.'s (2021) table. Its correspondence with the mammalian biceps femoris is proposed but not settled — Diogo & Molnar (2014) treat the hamstring group as deriving from the ischioflexorius field rather than from a single iliofibularis.
homology.openQuestion: Is the amniote iliofibularis the homologue of the mammalian biceps femoris, or does the hamstring group derive wholesale from the ischioflexorius field?
homology.teaching: A muscle spanning hip and knee whose declining leverage is measurable along the bird line — a case where a function claim rests on geometry, not on presence or absence.

muscles.name: Femorotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.
synonyms: vastus lateralis + vastus medialis + vastus intermedius (mammals)

consensus.insertion: Tibia, via the knee extensor apparatus.
consensus.action: Extends the knee. Because it does not cross the hip, it is a pure knee extensor.

occurrences.note: Not separated from the extensor iliotibialis in salamanders under the Gadow/Walker/Diogo & Molnar reading.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy origin along the entire femoral shaft; joins the iliotibialis tendon to insert on the cnemial crest. Knee extensor, active in both stance and swing.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Externus arises fleshy about a third of the way down the dorsal femur and inserts on the proximo-lateral cnemial crest; internus arises by tendon on the dorso-proximal femur, distal and anterior to iliofemoralis, and joins the same tendon at insertion.

occurrences.name: M. femorotibialis lateralis + medialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian femorotibialis externus and internus.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
occurrences.origin: Greater trochanter, linea aspera, and anterior/lateral femoral shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Patella, then the tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament.

homology.notes: The femorotibialis → vasti correspondence is one of the least contested in the hindlimb. Together with the rectus femoris (from extensor iliotibialis) it forms the mammalian quadriceps — a composite of two different ancestral muscles, which is why the rectus femoris crosses the hip and the vasti do not.
homology.teaching: Explains a fact students memorise without understanding: why one of the four quadriceps heads flexes the hip and three do not. They are not four parts of one muscle; they are two muscles.

muscles.name: 'Ambiens'
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Romer (1942) and Jones (1979) emphasise that it is a DORSAL muscle despite its ventral position.

consensus.insertion: Tibia (and in some archosaurs, via the digital flexor tendons).
consensus.action: Protracts the femur and extends the knee.

occurrences.note: Not present as a separate muscle; part of the undivided extensor iliotibialis.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.note: Reptiles may have both an 'ambiens' and a 'pubifemoralis'; the two names are sometimes used as synonyms (Russell & Bauer 2008), which is a persistent source of confusion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle has dorsal and ventral heads; the dorsal attaches to the ventral edge of the acetabulum and the ventral lies anteriorly, both converging on the femur at the intertrochanteric fossa.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tendinous origin on the proximo-lateral pubis, becoming tendinous distally along the anterior surface.

occurrences.name: M. ambiens
occurrences.note: In birds the ambiens tendon famously passes to the digital flexors, an arrangement once invoked (incorrectly) as an automatic perching mechanism. Hip flexor and knee extensor; the name is retained across the transition.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar reject the classical derivation of the mammalian sartorius from the 'ambiens'; they derive the sartorius from the anterior head of puboischiofemoralis internus (Walker & Homberger 1997).

homology.notes: The critical diagnostic is that the 'ambiens' is a DORSAL muscle sitting in a ventral position. The amphibian 'pubifemoralis', which looks superficially similar in dorsal view, is a deep VENTRAL muscle and corresponds instead to the reptilian adductor femoris. Diogo & Molnar make this call explicitly and reject the ambiens→sartorius derivation.
homology.teaching: A worked example of using mass assignment (dorsal vs ventral) rather than position to settle a homology dispute.

muscles.name: Adductor femoris
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral mass.
synonyms: adductor magnus + adductor longus + adductor brevis (mammals)

consensus.origin: Ventral surface of the pelvic girdle (pubis and ischium).
consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the femur.
consensus.action: Adducts and retracts the femur.
consensus.innervation: Obturator nerve (with a sciatic contribution to the adductor magnus in mammals).

occurrences.name: 'Pubifemoralis'
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar's dissections support the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' = reptilian adductor femoris, against the alternative that it corresponds to the 'ambiens'. Both are deep ventral muscles lying just dorsal to the pubotibialis and running from the ventral girdle to the ventral femur; the 'ambiens' is dorsal.
occurrences.origin: Anterior and ventral surface of the pubo-ischiac plate, anterior to the puboischiofemoralis externus.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral face of the femur, anterior and distal to the puboischiofemoralis externus but posterior to the puboischiofemoralis internus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. pubifemoralis. The three ventral pelvis-to-femur muscles are separated by their sequence along the femur rather than by distinct attachment sites — internus anterior, pubifemoralis next, externus posterior.

occurrences.name: Adductor femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the puboischiadic ligament to the ventral femoral shaft; adducts and protracts the femur, active in both stance and swing.

occurrences.name: M. puboischiofemoralis medialis + lateralis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian adductor femoris 1 and 2 respectively.

occurrences.name: Adductor magnus, longus and brevis
occurrences.origin: Inferior pubic ramus and ischial tuberosity.
occurrences.insertion: Linea aspera and adductor tubercle of the femur.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve (L2–L4); the hamstring part of adductor magnus by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar note that almost all amphibian–reptile ventral pelvic/thigh homologies are straightforward and consensual, with exactly two exceptions: the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' and 'ischiofemoralis'. They resolve both — pubifemoralis = adductor femoris, ischiofemoralis = ischiotrochantericus.

muscles.name: Ischiotrochantericus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.

consensus.insertion: Trochanteric region of the proximal femur.
consensus.action: Laterally rotates the femur; stabilises the hip.
consensus.innervation: Sacral plexus branches; nerve to obturator internus in mammals.

occurrences.name: 'Ischiofemoralis'
occurrences.note: Most authors (and Diogo & Molnar) hold that the amphibian 'ischiofemoralis' corresponds to the reptilian ischiotrochantericus; Gadow (1882) was a minority voice for adductor femoris. Walker (1954, p. 94) defends the ischiotrochantericus reading.
occurrences.origin: Lateral border of the ischium — the posterior portion of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior face of the head of the femur.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. ischiofemoralis, and the passage that fixes the plate's composition: the paper equates the ischium with the plate's posterior portion, which is what licenses scoring the plate as pubis plus ischium throughout.

occurrences.name: M. ischiofemoralis
occurrences.note: Hip extensor and lateral rotator.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus (+ gemelli)
occurrences.origin: Internal surface of the obturator membrane and adjacent ischium and pubis.
occurrences.insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter.
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh.
occurrences.divisionNote: The gemelli are claimed by this field and by the puboischiofemoralis externus; the dataset records both claims.

homology.notes: One of the two contested amphibian ventral pelvic muscles resolved by Diogo & Molnar (the other being 'pubifemoralis').

muscles.name: Puboischiotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.
synonyms: puboischiotibialis sensu Mivart 1869 and Iordansky & Morozov 1994

consensus.origin: Ventral pelvic girdle — pubis and ischium.
consensus.insertion: Medial surface of the proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.origin: Pubo-ischiac plate, lateral to the midline.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior surface of the tibia.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The most superficial muscle over the pelvis in ventral view, divided into proximal and distal sections by a tendinous inscription at about the level of the acetabulum. Francis (1934) and Mivart (1869) describe it as an undivided sheet in Salamandra and Cryptobranchus, so the inscription is not general to salamanders.
occurrences.divisionNote: Divided into proximal and distal sections by a tendinous inscription at about the level of the acetabulum in Taricha. Francis (1934) and Mivart (1869) describe it as an undivided sheet in Salamandra and Cryptobranchus, so the inscription is not general to salamanders.

occurrences.name: Gracilis major + gracilis minor
occurrences.note: Two heads in anurans versus one in mammals. Both derive from the puboischiotibialis, but via different heads — so the anuran and mammalian 'gracilis' are not straightforwardly equivalent. The anuran gracilis major is Mivart's and Iordansky & Morozov's puboischiotibialis (Přikryl et al. 2009).

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
occurrences.insertion: Superior medial tibia (pes anserinus).
occurrences.action: Adducts the thigh; flexes and medially rotates the leg.
occurrences.divisionNote: One head, against two in anurans (Prikryl et al. 2009).

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar single out the gracilis as the one muscle for which the last common ancestor of tetrapods probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — the muscles printed in bold in their Table 1. Every other human hindlimb muscle is a subdivision or recombination.
homology.teaching: A one-line answer to 'which of my leg muscles would a salamander recognise?' — essentially just the gracilis.

muscles.name: Ischioflexorius / flexor tibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.
synonyms: semitendinosus + semimembranosus + biceps femoris (mammals — the hamstrings)

consensus.insertion: Proximal tibia and/or fibula; in some taxa continuing to the tarsus.
consensus.action: Flexes the knee and retracts (extends) the hip.

occurrences.name: Ischioflexorius
occurrences.origin: Posterior and lateral edge of the ischium, behind the puboischiotibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar aponeurosis overlying the flexor primordialis communis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Runs from the pelvis to the sole without a bony insertion — the longest muscle chain in the hindlimb, and one whose action cannot be read from any single joint.
occurrences.note: Only the distal section is fully separable from the puboischiotibialis in Taricha; the proximal section is incompletely divided from it and resists mechanical separation. Pseudoeurycea, Bolitoglossa, Paramesotriton and Onychodactylus share this. The character does not follow salamander phylogeny and must have arisen or been lost more than once.

occurrences.name: 'Semitendinosus'
occurrences.note: A false-friend name. The anuran 'semitendinosus' is not homologous to the mammalian muscle of that name. Přikryl et al. (2009) record that the anuran 'semimembranosus' was called ischioflexorius by Hoffmann and caudalipuboischiotibialis by Francis, while the anuran 'semitendinosus' was called ischioflexorius by Mivart and puboischiotibialis by Hoffmann. Two muscles, four names, two of them shared — which is what Diogo & Molnar mean by false friends.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor tibialis internus is four-part in Crocodylus: FTI1 from the postero-lateral ischium to the proximo-medial tibia by a long tendon shared with puboischiotibialis; FTI2 fleshy from the postero-ventral ilium; FTI3 from the proximo-lateral ischium.

occurrences.name: M. flexor cruris medialis + flexor cruris lateralis pars pelvica
occurrences.note: = crocodylian flexor tibialis internus 3 and flexor tibialis externus. Crocodylian flexor tibialis internus 1 is LOST between Avialae and Aves — one of the few outright losses in their table.

occurrences.name: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris
occurrences.origin: Ischial tuberosity; the short head of biceps femoris from the linea aspera.
occurrences.insertion: Medial tibia (semitendinosus, semimembranosus); head of the fibula (biceps femoris).
occurrences.action: Extend the hip and flex the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular division.

nerves.note: Only the short head of biceps femoris. It is the one hamstring on the dorsal division, which is why the muscle's nerve and its ventral-mass identity disagree here — a real exception, not a scoring error.

homology.notes: The hamstring group derives from this field, but the correspondences head-by-head are not settled. Diogo & Molnar reject the classical claim (Gregory & Camp 1918; Romer 1922; Haines 1935) that the mammalian tenuissimus is the caudal head of biceps femoris; following Jones (1979) they derive tenuissimus from a dorsal tail-region muscle homologous with the reptilian 'flexor cruris tarsi dorsalis'.

serial.caution: Frequently asserted; the two are innervated by different divisions and derive from opposite masses (hamstrings ventral, triceps dorsal). This correspondence should be treated as functional analogy.

homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.origin: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament.
consensus.insertion: Gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial tract.
consensus.action: Extends and laterally rotates the hip; principal muscle of the erect-posture power stroke.

occurrences.name: Gluteus maximus
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar note innervation differences between humans and rats: the human gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve alone, the rat muscle by that nerve plus the inferior branch of the superior gluteal nerve. One of several cases where innervation differs between mammals for muscles otherwise treated as identical.

occurrences.name: 'Gluteus maximus'
occurrences.note: A false-friend name. The anuran muscle called 'gluteus maximus' is not homologous to the mammalian one; Diogo & Molnar use 'extensor iliotibialis B' instead.
The enlargement of this field along the synapsid stem is part of the erect-posture transition documented by Bishop & Pierce.
occurrences.name: Gluteal (dorsal iliac) mass

homology.notes: A mammalian differentiation from the dorsal iliac field. Its name is applied to non-homologous muscles in the anuran literature — one of the clearest cases in Diogo & Molnar's list of false-friend names ('tensor fasciae latae', 'gluteus maximus', 'gemellus', 'obturator externus', 'quadratus femoris', 'obturator internus', 'pectineus', 'adductor longus', 'iliacus', 'sartorius', 'semitendinosus', 'adductor magnus' — none homologous in anurans to the human muscles of the same name).
homology.teaching: The anchor for the false-friend-names lesson. Twelve human muscle names are applied to non-homologous anuran muscles.

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Distal femur, by medial and lateral heads (and from the tibia in some taxa).
consensus.insertion: Calcaneum/fibulare, via the Achilles tendon.
consensus.action: Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.note: Walthall & Ashley-Ross describe no discrete gastrocnemius in Taricha. The flexor primordialis communis occupies the position and takes the femoral epicondylar origin that the amniote gastrocnemius takes, and the paper treats it as one muscle. Recorded here without changing the presence state, since other sources score a gastrocnemius in Caudata; what this source shows is that the boundary between the two is a division that not every author makes.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.action: The principal jump-propulsion muscle; hypertrophied relative to all other anuran leg muscles.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the ventral proximal tibia and the distal ventral tibial crest, by a broad aponeurosis onto the proximolateral margins of the first three phalanges — not onto a calcaneum, unlike the mammalian condition.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Externus arises by a tendon shared with the caudofemoralis longus and from the posterolateral femoral epicondyle, which bears a scattered striated surface; internus from the proximoposterior tibia. Both insert on the calcaneum by a broad tendon.

occurrences.name: M. gastrocnemius
occurrences.note: Ankle plantarflexor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.origin: Medial and lateral femoral condyles.
occurrences.insertion: Calcaneal tuberosity via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
occurrences.action: Plantarflexes the foot; flexes the knee.
occurrences.note: Kardong (2002) derived the mammalian gastrocnemius from the femorotibial ('internal') head; Diogo & Molnar discuss and qualify this.

homology.notes: Universal across Tetrapoda. Head count and the femoral versus tibial origin vary.

serial.caution: The crural and antebrachial flexor masses correspond as fields, but muscle-for-muscle mapping within them is unreliable.

muscles.name: Tibialis anterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Proximal tibia and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Medial tarsals and the base of metatarsal I.
consensus.action: Dorsiflexes the ankle; inverts the foot.

occurrences.name: Extensor cruris tibialis
occurrences.origin: Tibial (medial) epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Extensively on the anterodorsal and anteroventral faces of the tibia.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. extensor cruris tibialis. Visible from both ventral and dorsal views as it fans from the femoral epicondyle across the anterior face of the tibia — three rows for one muscle on one bone, because it wraps.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the proximomedial tibia to the dorsolateral proximal metatarsals I-II; the metatarsal bases carry coarse rugosities marking the insertion.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis (classical) / extensor digitorum longus (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)
occurrences.note: Which avian muscle this record corresponds to is exactly what Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) dispute. Scored uncertain rather than picking a side.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Lateral condyle and proximal lateral tibia; interosseous membrane.
occurrences.insertion: Medial cuneiform and base of metatarsal I.

homology.notes: Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) propose that the classical homologies of the two anterior tibial muscles are swapped: on their reading the avian m. tibialis cranialis is homologous with the NON-AVIAN m. extensor digitorum longus, and the avian m. extensor digitorum longus with the non-avian m. tibialis anterior. Their argument is that this requires no drastic change in attachment sites between avian and non-avian homologues, whereas the classical scheme does. The classical scheme descends from Romer (1923-27) and, they note, had been used uncritically by palaeontologists for a century. Their method weights morphological and functional congruence over innervation, on the grounds that nerve-muscle specificity is itself variable across taxa — which is the reverse of the priority used elsewhere in this dataset, and worth noting as a genuine methodological disagreement rather than a detail. Allen et al. (2021) independently adopt the revised scheme in their crocodylian-to-avian homology table, equating the crocodylian extensor digitorum longus with the avian m. tibialis cranialis. That is a second line of support for Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading against the classical one, from authors working on moment arms rather than on homology, so the agreement is not circular.
homology.openQuestion: Is the avian tibialis cranialis the homologue of the non-avian tibialis anterior (Romer's scheme, followed by most of the literature) or of the non-avian extensor digitorum longus (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)? The two schemes imply different attachment histories across the archosaur stem, so fossil muscle reconstruction in theropods depends on which is right.

muscles.name: Extensor digitorum longus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Lateral tibial condyle, proximal fibula and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the toes; dorsiflexes the ankle.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the femur, anterior to the extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis; sometimes a few fibres from the tibial spine.
occurrences.insertion: Bases of the metatarsals, by many small tendons.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thin, lying on the dorsal crus between the extensor tarsi tibialis and the extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis. Unlike its forelimb counterpart it stops at the metatarsals rather than reaching the phalanges.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: From the lateral femoral extensor fossa and condyle to the proximodorsal metatarsals III-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the lateral femoral extensor fossa and lateral condyle onto the proximodorsal metatarsals III-IV, which bear a smooth bump at the insertion. Note that this is a femoral origin, not a tibial one — relevant to the Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) dispute over which anterior tibial muscle is which.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: See the tibialis anterior record: which avian muscle is the homologue is disputed.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Lateral tibial condyle, anterior fibula, interosseous membrane.
occurrences.insertion: Extensor expansions of digits II–V.
occurrences.note: In humans the fibularis tertius derives from the extensor digitorum longus anlage (Lewis 1910). In rats the fibularis digiti quinti derives from the extensor digiti quinti anlage. The two are therefore NOT homologous, despite both being called a 'fibularis' and both being innervated by the deep fibular nerve.

homology.notes: The muscle itself is straightforward; the interest is in its derivatives. The human fibularis tertius / rat fibularis digiti quinti case is one of Diogo & Molnar's cleanest demonstrations that shared name plus shared nerve still does not establish homology. Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) propose that the classical homologies of the two anterior tibial muscles are swapped: on their reading the avian m. tibialis cranialis is homologous with the NON-AVIAN m. extensor digitorum longus, and the avian m. extensor digitorum longus with the non-avian m. tibialis anterior. Their argument is that this requires no drastic change in attachment sites between avian and non-avian homologues, whereas the classical scheme does. The classical scheme descends from Romer (1923-27) and, they note, had been used uncritically by palaeontologists for a century. Their method weights morphological and functional congruence over innervation, on the grounds that nerve-muscle specificity is itself variable across taxa — which is the reverse of the priority used elsewhere in this dataset, and worth noting as a genuine methodological disagreement rather than a detail. Allen et al. (2021) independently adopt the revised scheme in their crocodylian-to-avian homology table, equating the crocodylian extensor digitorum longus with the avian m. tibialis cranialis. That is a second line of support for Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading against the classical one, from authors working on moment arms rather than on homology, so the agreement is not circular.

serial.note: In rats, the short extensors of digits 2 and 3 are fused in BOTH limbs — extensor indicis in the forelimb, extensor digitorum brevis in the hindlimb. Diogo & Molnar show these fusions are independently derived, producing apparent serial similarity by parallelism.

homology.teaching: The rat double-fusion case is the single most economical illustration of parallelism masquerading as serial homology.

muscles.name: Fibularis (peroneus) group
muscles.developmental: Somitic; lateral compartment of the crus, dorsal mass.
synonyms: peroneus longus / brevis / tertius / digiti quinti

consensus.insertion: Metatarsals and lateral tarsals.
consensus.action: Everts the foot; plantarflexes (longus, brevis) or dorsiflexes (tertius).
consensus.innervation: Superficial fibular nerve (longus, brevis); deep fibular nerve (tertius, digiti quinti).

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Both insert on the anterior surface of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibularis longus arises on the fibular shaft distal to the iliofibular tubercle; brevis from the distal fibular shaft and the anterior tibial aponeurosis. Both insert on the anterior surface of metatarsal V.

occurrences.name: M. fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Names retained; longus plantarflexes, brevis dorsiflexes.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus, brevis (+ tertius in humans, digiti quinti in rats)
occurrences.action: Evert the foot; the longus also supports the transverse arch.
occurrences.innervation: Superficial fibular nerve (L5–S1) for longus and brevis.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar dwell on this group because the innervation is diagnostic and cuts against the obvious grouping. The fibularis tertius and fibularis digiti quinti are innervated by the DEEP fibular nerve — which supplies short extensors such as extensor digitorum brevis — not by the superficial fibular nerve that supplies the true lateral muscles fibularis longus and brevis. Deriving them from the lateral mass would require the innervation to have changed; deriving them from the extensor anlage does not.
homology.openQuestion: Diogo & Molnar state explicitly that a firm answer requires a much more extensive analysis including innervation and developmental data.
homology.teaching: Innervation as a decisive argument. Two muscles sit in the lateral compartment and carry a lateral-compartment name, but their nerve says they belong to the extensor group.

muscles.name: Popliteus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; derived from the interosseus cruris.

consensus.insertion: Posterior proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Unlocks the extended knee by rotating the tibia; medially rotates the leg.

homology.notes: The popliteus derives from the interosseus cruris.

serial.caution: This is Diogo & Molnar's headline counter-example. The popliteus and pronator teres are frequently listed as forelimb–hindlimb topological equivalents, but they derive from DIFFERENT anlagen: popliteus from the interosseus cruris, pronator teres from the flexor antebrachii et carpi radialis. The true ontogenetic counterparts are hindlimb tibialis posterior and forelimb palmaris profundus / pronator profundus.

homology.teaching: The cleanest single case for separating topological correspondence from developmental correspondence. Worth teaching verbatim.

muscles.name: Tibialis posterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Interosseous membrane and the adjacent tibia and fibula.
consensus.insertion: Navicular, cuneiforms and the bases of the middle metatarsals.
consensus.action: Inverts the foot; plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch.

serial.note: Diogo & Molnar identify hindlimb tibialis posterior and forelimb palmaris profundus / pronator profundus (pronator quadratus) as the REAL ontogenetic counterparts — as against the popliteus/pronator teres pairing, which is topological only.

homology.teaching: The positive half of the popliteus lesson: this is what a developmentally supported correspondence looks like.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum longus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass of the crus.

consensus.insertion: Plantar surfaces of the distal phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the toes; plantarflexes the ankle.

occurrences.name: Flexor primordialis communis
occurrences.origin: Chiefly the posteroventral face of the fibula, with part arising by tendon from the fibular epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar aponeurosis, which divides into five tendons to the proximal end of the terminal phalanx of each digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. flexor primordialis communis. Five tendons, against four in the hand — the pes retains digit V. Its function is given as pressing the sole against the ground rather than flexing the digits.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the lateral femoral epicondyle; distally a stout tendon serving digits I-IV. Ankle plantarflexor, active in stance.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Femoral origin; inserts on the proximoventral unguals I-III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the ventral distal femur and lateral condyle, which carries parallel striae aligned with the femoral long axis, onto the proximoventral unguals I-III.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Together with the flexor hallucis longus, forms the tendon system that produces automatic toe flexion when the ankle flexes — the mechanism of perching. Ankle plantarflexor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Posterior tibia.
occurrences.insertion: Distal phalanges of digits II–V.

serial.note: Among the strongest forelimb–hindlimb correspondences. Diogo & Molnar's Fig. 3 shows that the distal (zeugopodial and autopodial) muscles of the salamander fore and hind limbs are strikingly similar, while the proximal (girdle and stylopodial) muscles are clearly different.

homology.teaching: The distal-greater-than-proximal similarity gradient is visible in a single salamander dissection.

muscles.name: Flexores breves superficiales (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Middle phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the toes at the metatarsophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.origin: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
occurrences.insertion: For digits II-V, the ventral side of the distal ends of the metatarsals and the ventral surface of the proximal end of the proximal phalanx; for digit I, the distal end of the metatarsal only.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tripartite for every digit except the first, which lacks the phalangeal connection. The manus counterpart differs: there the slips flank the metacarpals of digits II and III but not I and IV.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.note: A single muscular body in Triprion despite the plural name, on the lateroplantar tarsus beneath the aponeurosis plantaris.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Despite the plural name, a single muscular body in Triprion, on the lateroplantar tarsal surface and ventrally concealed by the aponeurosis plantaris.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis superficialis
occurrences.note: Layer 1 of the seven-layer pedal scheme.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis superficialis, digits I-IV, from the ventral calcaneum with digit-specific variation. Layer 1 of the seven-layer pedal scheme Pereyra et al. set out.

serial.note: Part of the strongly corresponding distal muscle set.

muscles.name: Contrahentes digitorum (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges.
consensus.action: Adducts the toes toward the foot's axis.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.origin: The flat tendon of the caput longum musculorum contrahentium, and the tarsal bones.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal phalanx of each digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Passes from the tarsals along the ventral axis of the metatarsals. As in the hand, part of the origin is on the caput longum tendon rather than on bone.

occurrences.name: Mm. contrahentes digitorum pedis
occurrences.note: Blotto et al. (2020) record a full contrahens series in the anuran foot, including one serving the prehallux — the pedal counterpart of the prepollex contrahens in the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Blotto et al. record a full contrahens series in the anuran foot, including one serving the prehallux.

occurrences.name: Interdigiti dorsales + ventrales
occurrences.note: Running between successive metatarsals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The interdigiti dorsales and ventrales of Pereyra et al., running between successive metatarsals; their origins are marked by longitudinally oriented fine striae on the proximolateral metatarsal surfaces.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis
occurrences.note: As in the hand, the contrahens layer is largely lost in mammals, with the adductor hallucis surviving as its principal representative.

muscles.name: Flexores breves profundi (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deepest ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges and metatarsophalangeal sesamoids.
consensus.action: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joints; abducts and adducts the toes.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores breves profundi
occurrences.note: Includes slips serving the prehallux.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis profundus
occurrences.note: Deep flexor layer; metatarsal origins marked by fine striae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis profundus, digits I-IV, from metatarsals I-III and V and the distal calcaneum. The metatarsal origins are marked by fine striae — the pedal correlates Pereyra et al. identify for the first time.

occurrences.name: Interossei (plantar and dorsal)
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).

serial.note: One of the strongest distal correspondences: the same three-layer plantar/palmar system in both limbs.

muscles.name: Pubotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.origin: Anterior edge and anterior ventral face of the pelvis.
consensus.insertion: Anterior face of the proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Supports the body during walking and flexes the knee.
consensus.innervation: Ventral division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Pubotibialis
occurrences.origin: Anterior edge and anterior ventral face of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior face of the proximal end of the tibia.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its parallel fibres pass anterior to the puboischiotibialis to a proximal tibial insertion. Function attributed on the strength of Ashley-Ross (1995) electromyography in Dicamptodon, not inferred from geometry.

homology.notes: A pelvis-to-tibia muscle anterior to the puboischiotibialis. Its relation to the amniote ambiens is not established here.

muscles.name: Femorofibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.origin: Ventral face of the distal end of the femur.
consensus.insertion: Posterolateral face of the fibula.
consensus.action: Flexes the knee.
consensus.innervation: Ventral division of the lumbosacral plexus; branches of the same nerve serve the distal ischioflexorius.

occurrences.name: Femorofibularis
occurrences.origin: Ventral face of the distal end of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Posterolateral face of the fibula.
occurrences.note: Robust in Taricha, against the thin narrow muscle usual in salamanders. Ashley-Ross (1992) found a size trade-off with the ischioflexorius: Dicamptodon and newly metamorphosed Ambystoma have a large ischioflexorius and a slender femorofibularis, older Ambystoma the reverse, and Darevsky & Salomatina (1989) report the same trade-off in Paramesotriton. Francis (1934) noted that branches of one nerve supply the distal ischioflexorius and the femorofibularis, which is the basis for treating them as alternative solutions to one mechanical demand. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A short femur-to-fibula strap crossing only the knee, against the ischioflexorius which runs from the pelvis to the sole. Two muscles of very different span substituting for one another in size is a caution against reading function from length.

homology.teaching: A reciprocal size relationship between two muscles that share a nerve branch but not a span. The trade-off shows up across species and within one species across ontogeny.
homology.notes: No amniote counterpart is established. Shared innervation with the distal ischioflexorius is the strongest evidence bearing on its identity.

muscles.name: Caudalipuboischiotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal hypaxial series recruited to the hindlimb.

consensus.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
consensus.insertion: The tendinous inscription dividing the puboischiotibialis.
consensus.action: Assists the puboischiotibialis in limb retraction and flexes the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Caudalipuboischiotibialis
occurrences.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
occurrences.insertion: The tendinous inscription dividing the proximal and distal portions of the puboischiotibialis — not bone.
occurrences.note: Coactive with the puboischiotibialis during walking (Ashley-Ross 1995). Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A muscle with a skeletal origin and no skeletal insertion: it ends on another muscle's tendinous inscription. Salamandra and Cryptobranchus lack that inscription altogether, so in those genera the insertion has nothing to attach to.

homology.notes: One of three tail-to-pelvis muscles. Its insertion on a tendinous inscription rather than bone means it cannot be reconstructed from a skeleton.

muscles.name: Iliocaudalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal epaxial series reaching the pelvic girdle.

consensus.insertion: Ilium.
consensus.action: Draws the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Iliocaudalis
occurrences.origin: The first several caudal vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Ilium.
occurrences.note: Its fibres run parallel to the epaxial muscles and it is distinguishable from them only by its insertion. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A muscle identified by where it ends rather than by any visible boundary — the clearest case in this source of an attachment doing the work of delimiting a muscle.

homology.teaching: Where a muscle has no visible border with its neighbours, its insertion is the only thing that makes it a muscle at all.

muscles.name: Ischiocaudalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal hypaxial series reaching the pelvic girdle.

consensus.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
consensus.insertion: Posterior border of the ischium.
consensus.action: Draws the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Ischiocaudalis
occurrences.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior border of the ischium.
occurrences.note: The most medial of the three ventral muscles connecting tail and pelvic girdle. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flat, thin and strap-like. With the caudalipuboischiotibialis and caudofemoralis it forms a series of three, all from the anterior caudal transverse processes, differing in where they end.

muscles.name: Extensor tarsi tibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the tibiale.
consensus.action: Supinates the foot.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Extensor tarsi tibialis
occurrences.origin: Tibial epicondyle of the femur, next to the extensor cruris tibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral surface of the tibiale.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crosses knee and ankle to reach a proximal tarsal. Function presumed from geometry, not measured.

muscles.name: Extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.insertion: Posterodorsal and posteroventral faces of the fibula, with a portion on the fibulare.
consensus.action: Extends the knee.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis
occurrences.origin: Fibular epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Much of the posterodorsal and posteroventral faces of the fibula, with a portion inserting on the fibulare.
occurrences.note: The postaxial complement of the extensor cruris tibialis: the two wrap the tibia and fibula respectively from the two femoral epicondyles. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Three rows on two bones for one muscle, because it wraps the fibula from dorsal to ventral and continues onto the proximal tarsus.

muscles.name: Interosseus cruris
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep layer between the zeugopodial elements.

consensus.insertion: Distal portion of the tibia.
consensus.action: Stabilises the two long bones of the crus against one another.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.origin: Proximal part of the fibula, on the medial side.
occurrences.insertion: Distal portion of the tibia.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Joins the medial sides of tibia and fibula. Its serial counterpart in the forelimb is the pronator profundus, which in salamanders runs the other way — from the ulna across to the radial side — and acts as a pronator rather than a strut.

homology.notes: Occupies the position of the amniote interosseous membrane as a muscle rather than a ligament.

muscles.name: Pronator profundus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Lateral face of the distal tibia, the tibiale, and the base of the first metatarsal.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Pronator profundus
occurrences.origin: Medial side of the fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral face of the distal end of the tibia, the tibiale, and the base of the first metatarsal.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Roughly triangular, converging from the postaxial to the preaxial side of the ankle — the same crossing course as its counterpart in the hand.

homology.notes: Walthall & Ashley-Ross give the same name to this muscle and to its counterpart in the hand, which is why the two are separate records here.

muscles.name: Contrahentium caput longum (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: A flat tendon attaching to the distal tarsal bones.
consensus.action: Flexes the tarsus.

occurrences.name: Caput longum musculorum contrahentium
occurrences.origin: Distal portion of the fibula, on the medial side.
occurrences.insertion: A flat tendon attaching to the distal tarsal bones.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thin, lying deep to the plantar fascia. Its insertion tendon is in turn the origin of the contrahentes digitorum, the same chained arrangement the hand shows.

occurrences.name: Contrahentium caput longum
occurrences.attachmentNote: A single muscle from the medial ligamentum calcanei, inserting fleshily along the distal three-quarters of the ventral tibiale, independent of the tibialis posterior.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

homology.notes: Separated from the forelimb record of the same name because Blotto et al. (2020) and Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006) both describe hand and foot muscles under this one name.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis
occurrences.origin: Lateral edge of the fibulare.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibres run diagonally toward the anterior side of the foot. The forelimb counterpart takes the distal ulna as well as the carpals; this one is confined to the tarsus.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius medialis (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.origin: Distal fibula, the fibulare and the intermedium.
consensus.insertion: Plantar fascia.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius medialis
occurrences.origin: Distal region of the fibula, the fibulare and the intermedium.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar fascia.
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Parallel to the lateral accessory and sharing its insertion, differing only in taking a more proximal origin that reaches the fibula.

muscles.name: Intermetatarsales
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Metatarsal of the adjacent digit.
consensus.action: Adducts the metatarsals and the digits attached to them.

occurrences.name: Intermetatarsales
occurrences.origin: Metatarsals of adjacent digits.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsals of adjacent digits.
occurrences.note: These muscles form the web-like structures between the digits. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Extend further distally on the fibular side of each metatarsal — an asymmetry the intermetacarpales of the hand do not show.

muscles.name: Extensores digitorum breves (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.origin: Distal tarsals at the base of each digit.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx, by long tendons.
consensus.action: Extends the digits.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.origin: Distal tarsal bones at the base of each digit.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx of each digit, by a long tendon.
occurrences.note: Five slips, one per digit. The muscular part reaches only about two-thirds along the metatarsal; the tendon continues to the terminal phalanx. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Five slips against three in the manus, which serves digits II-IV only. The difference is the salamander hand's missing digit V, not a difference in the muscle layer.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Extensor digitorum brevis superficialis arises from the astragalar hollow and lateral calcaneum; the deep layer arises from the proximodorsal metatarsals, whose fine striations run parallel to the metatarsal long axis.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

muscles.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal intrinsic layer of the pes, preaxial margin.

consensus.origin: Proximal tarsals of the preaxial ankle.
consensus.insertion: Lateral face of the first metatarsal and its phalanx.
consensus.action: Abducts and extends the first metatarsal and its digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I
occurrences.origin: Intermedium and centrale.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral face of the first metatarsal, with a small slip to the phalanx.
occurrences.note: The paper's text calls these 'bones of the wrist' in the hindlimb section, evidently a slip for the ankle; the muscle is figured in the pes. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The preaxial counterpart of the abductor digiti minimi at the other margin of the foot. Its forelimb equivalent takes the radiale and intermedium.

muscles.name: Abductor digiti minimi (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; intrinsic layer of the pes, postaxial margin.

consensus.insertion: Fibulare, the postaxial distal tarsal, and the base of the fifth metatarsal.
consensus.action: Abducts the fifth metatarsal and its digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti V
occurrences.origin: Ventral surface of the distal end of the fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Fleshy attachment to the posterior side of the fibulare, basale V, and the base of the fifth metatarsal.
occurrences.note: Basale V is scored as a distal tarsal; the paper's more specific term is kept here rather than given its own element. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: An extensive fleshy insertion across three skeletal elements. The manus counterpart serves digit IV, because the salamander hand has lost digit V — the same muscle at the same margin, on a differently numbered digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti minimi
occurrences.attachmentNote: A large muscle with fleshy origin over almost the whole dorsolateral fibulare, inserting by short tendon on the dorsal and proximal metatarsal V.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

homology.teaching: Postaxial position and digit number disagree between hand and foot in salamanders. Matching by number would pair this muscle with nothing; matching by position pairs it with the manual extensor lateralis digiti IV.
